name: Spearmint (tea, extract or oil)
short: Testosterone fell in women with PCOS on spearmint tea; a case report links the oil to lip allergy. A 90-day extract trial found no severe adverse events, but earlier studies conflict on toxicity.
text: Safety evidence is limited. A randomised placebo-controlled trial of a dried water extract of spearmint taken for 90 days by healthy adults with age-associated memory impairment found no severe adverse events, no significant difference between groups in the number of people reporting adverse effects, and no effect on follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone or thyroid-stimulating hormone levels, vital signs or blood tests (the abstract does not report testosterone); its abstract also notes that earlier studies of spearmint extracts in humans and animals reported conflicting results on toxicity. In a 30-day randomised trial in which 42 women with polycystic ovary syndrome took spearmint tea twice a day or a placebo herbal tea, free and total testosterone fell significantly and LH and FSH rose in the spearmint tea group, so it may change hormone levels; the abstract does not give the between-group comparison for hormones and does not report on adverse events. For the oil, one case report is titled as allergic contact cheilitis (lip inflammation) from spearmint oil; the record has no abstract, so no further details are available. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
